title: Processors, Parallel Processing and Virtual Machines
overview: This topic extends CPU architecture to processor design choices, instruction pipelining, parallel architectures and virtual machines. The key is not memorising labels but explaining performance trade-offs and why a particular architecture suits a workload.
syllabusPoints: Compare RISC and CISC processor characteristics.
Explain pipelining and how branches/interrupts can disrupt it.
Describe SISD, SIMD, MISD and MIMD architectures and massively parallel systems.
Explain virtual machines, their uses, benefits and limitations.

definitions.definition: Reduced Instruction Set Computer: a small set of simple, usually fixed-format instructions.
Complex Instruction Set Computer: a larger set of more complex instructions/addressing modes.
Overlapping stages of several instruction executions to increase throughput.
Single Instruction Multiple Data: the same instruction operates on many data items in parallel.
Multiple Instruction Multiple Data: processors execute different instructions on different data.
A software-created computer environment that behaves as a separate machine while sharing host hardware.

sections.title: RISC versus CISC
content: RISC favours simple instructions, many registers and predictable instruction formats, which can support efficient pipelining. CISC can perform more work per instruction and reduce instruction count, but decoding/execution is more complex. 'RISC is faster' is not a sufficient evaluation by itself.

sections.title: Pipelining
content: Fetch, decode and execute for different instructions overlap. Once full, the pipeline can improve throughput because several instructions are in progress. A branch or interrupt may invalidate prefetched instructions, forcing a flush/refill and reducing the gain.

sections.title: Flynn-style architectures
content: SISD is conventional one-instruction/one-data processing. SIMD applies one instruction to many data items, useful for image/vector workloads. MISD is rare. MIMD allows multiple processors/cores to run different instructions on different data and is common in parallel systems.

sections.title: Massively parallel computing
content: A very large number of processing units operate simultaneously on decomposed parts of a problem. It excels when work can be parallelised, but communication, synchronisation, load balancing and serial sections limit speed-up.

sections.title: Virtual machines
content: A hypervisor/virtualisation layer lets multiple guest systems share hardware. Benefits include isolation, testing, snapshots, server consolidation and running different operating systems. Costs include overhead, resource contention and dependence on the host/hypervisor.

examTips: Identify both instruction streams and data streams in SIMD/MIMD questions.
Explain WHY pipelining improves throughput and mention hazards/flushes.
Give a concrete VM use such as isolated testing or running a different OS.
commonMistakes: Confusing multicore with SIMD; multicore commonly supports MIMD.
Saying pipelining makes one instruction execute instantly.
Saying VMs have separate physical processors/memory by definition.
